item.title: Rad Gifts That Fund the Fight: EFF's Holiday Merch Guide for 2026
item.description:
EFF supporters are why our lawyers can sue the government when it spies on you and chills your free speech. EFF members make it possible for our technologists to build the tools to protect privacy on the streets and online. And donations to EFF are what fuels our activists as they fight to pass good laws and to end bad company practices. But you can also support EFF by buying gear from the EFF Online Shop! And starting today, take 20% off your entire order with coupon code: "BL4CKFRID4Y" ! From now until midnight on Monday the 30th, stock up and stand out with rad, stylish EFF merch: Shop Now Support Digital Rights with Every Purchase What's New The Digital Unicorn was created for EFF's 25th anniversary, and it was too good to leave in the archives. It's back on the Digital Unicorn Tank Top to light the way to a brighter future: a soft black muscle tank in 100% combed and ring-spun cotton with a relaxed fit. Crows are very intelligent (and can even be trained!). Our Surveillance Is For the Birds Sticker depicts a murder of crows disabling a surveillance camera. EFF is fighting to end warrantless license plate reader mass surveillance—and we're going to win. But if they're going to take a picture, frame it for 'em with our Anti License Plate Reader (ALPR) Frame. It says, in raised lettering: "I Do Not Consent to the Tracking of This Vehicle," and includes an EFF logo. Shop Now Take 20% OFF with Code "BL4CKFRID4Y" What's Hot This embossed, tactile sticker depicts the fiery hair, sword, and scales of Lady Justice, with braille characters reading "justice" and "EFF." With this sticker you won't just show your support for a world where justice is available to everyone—you'll feel it. You can also bring a little texture to your favorite gear with the Circuit Brain Stim Sticker, printed with four layers of embossing for a noticeably raised tactile surface. The textured finish is as distinctive to touch as it is to see. And once your see our Motherboard Hooded Sweatshirt you'll know why it rounds out our list of the hottest items this year. It's got what our designers call "Lovelace-Klimtian" vibes. The same artwork is also available on the Scoop Neck Motherboard Shirt. For Your Next Party Our Liquid Core EFF Dice are perfect for tabletop games. Seven red resin dice with a glittery core in a clear-view metal tin, with the EFF logo on the D20. And they pair perfectly with the HTTP Code Playing Cards, designed by security expert, EFF board member, and competitive poker player Tarah Wheeler for the EFF benefit tournament at DEF CON. Every card carries an HTTP status code. Stocking Stuffers Under $20 Laptop Camera Cover Set: seven specially-designed stickers with a unique ultra-removable adhesive for reuse while preventing gummy residue—far better than masking tape! Perfect for a laptop, webcam, phone, tablet, and most other potential spying devices. "I Do Not Consent to the Search of This Device" sticker 3-pack is an evergreen reminder of your right to privacy in the digital world. This poop-emoji sticker is the literal depiction of EFF Advisor Cory Doctor's concept of enshittification. It's also available as an Enamel pin. Got a new laptop? Cover it in one go with the Privacy Sticker Combo, 30th Anniversary Sticker Combo, and the Multisticker Sheet Pack. Shop Now Support Digital Rights with Every Purchase Give Membership, Get a Thank-You Gift If you'd rather not guess sizes, an EFF Membership Gift Certificate arrives by email and redeems for a year of membership. The recipient picks their own gift at redemption—they get what they want, and you get the credit! And don't forget: Join EFF as a member to get a sticker sheet and a special "Claw Back" tee (or an EFF35 Cityscape tee). Order Early For delivery by December 25 in the continental U.S., order by December 10. Questions about sizes, shipping, or memberships? Please reach out to membership@eff.org. Thank you for supporting our mission and grabbing the perfect gifts for the digital rights defender in your life!

item.description:

He had tried to move to Costa Rica a year ago, but the Trump administration spent months trying to force him to move to Africa. [NY Times] * Trump's defamation case against the Times will move forward based on new standard that if the claimed crime is complex enough, it's inherently defamatory. [Slate] * Huawei convicted of sanctions violations. Too bad they couldn't get Trump to make a call for them. [Law360] * In the least shocking news ever, Donald Trump personally profited off of forcing Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang. [Popular Information] * Elon wants the Twitter fraud case thrown out, arguing that his public claims that he might abandon the deal didn't ultimately impact the sale price, which sort of glazes over the whole "the stock tanked until Twitter had to take legal action to force him to go through with the deal" bit. [Reuters] * Trump sanctions on the ICC struck down to the extent they sought to punish Americans working with the international human rights tribunal. item.title: Pluralistic: New York vs auto-enshittification (25 Nov 2026)
item.description:
Today's links New York vs auto-enshittification: A blueprint for states to fix Congress's mistake. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Homebrew DRM; HTML v regexp; Tesla-financial complex; Spain v Wall St landlords; "Cooking in Maximum Security." Upcoming appearances: Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal, Sheffield. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. New York vs auto-enshittification (permalink) As of February 27, 2027, it will be illegal for companies in New York to charge car-owners a subscription fee or an upcharge for any software feature that runs on hardware already installed in their car. It's a bold – if imperfect – disenshittification gambit aimed at the extremely (and increasingly) enshittified automotive industry: https://wgna.com/car-bill-extra-fees/ In a state of nature, there'd be no reason to pass a law like this. Say BMW decided to sell you a car that charged you a monthly subscription for the "feature" that auto-dipped your high-beams when there was an oncoming car (a thing BMW actually does): https://www.autoevolution.com/news/netizens-up-in-arms-over-bmw-adaptive-headlight-subscription-237335.html In a state of nature, BMW's sleazy scam would conjure forth competitors who would offer mechanics and drivers a one-click way to unlock the feature forever. Drivers would curse BMW and pay a one-time fee to get permanent access to the feature, and that would be the end of the matter. Indeed, the fact that this third-party fix could exist at all might well convince BMW not to bother with the high-beam scam in the first place (and if it didn't, well, then tinkerers, hackers, and entrepreneurs would swiftly obviate it). But we don't live in a state of nature. We live in a world with a federal "anticircumvention" law: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA 1201), which imposes a 5-year sentence and a $500k fine for this kind of reverse engineering, even if it does not result in a copyright infringement. There's no copyright law that says you can't change the software in your car to activate your high-beams' automatic controller, but that doesn't matter, because activating the controller without BMW's permission requires a reverse-engineering step and that's a felony. Jay Freeman rightly calls this "felony contempt of business model" because it lets companies send you to literal prison for doing otherwise legal things, just because it makes them unhappy. What's more, copyright is a firmly federal matter: copyright law "pre-empts" the states, meaning that states can't pass laws that modify federal copyright policy. That means that states can't override DMCA 1201 by legalizing reverse-engineering for otherwise lawful purposes (such as independent repair, performing software upgrades, or allowing generic consumables and parts). Anticircumvention is an attractive nuisance: it invites manufacturers to dream up as many scams as they can think of and then bury them in their products, secure in the knowledge that it is a literal felony to thwart their commercial plans. It's especially bad for cars, where anticircumvention is used: to block third-party parts and independent repair; to prevent drivers from preventing manufacturers, lenders and dealerships from spying on their driving habits, car informatics, and locations; to enable lenders (and hackers who break into dealerships' computers) to immobilize your car without any notice, appeal or due process: https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/24/rent-to-pwn/#kitt-is-a-demon The New York State bill (S.9348A/A.10411A) partially addresses some of these unfair and deceptive practices: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9348/amendment/A Before I get into what this law does (and doesn't) do, I want to get into how it does anything at all. Remember: anticircumvention was shoehorned into copyright law, and copyright is a federal matter. Copyright enjoys pre-emption, a ban on states' modifying it. At first blush, it seems like the states shouldn't be able to do anything about the enshittification that anticircumvention law enables. But the Right to Repair movement came up with a clever hack around pre-emption. States can't override federal copyright law, but state legislatures can regulate goods and services that are sold within their states. That means that states can simply ban the sale of goods that use anticircumvention to rip off or spy on the people who live within state limits. This is the basis for several successful Right to Repair laws, starting in 2022 with Colorado's powered wheelchair repair law (HB22-1031, cosponsored by the very excellent Brianna Titone): https://pluralistic.net/2022/06/08/chair-ish/#r2r This law does not purport to limit which copyrights the private-equity-backed powered wheelchair duopoly can exercise. It just orders anyone selling powered wheelchairs in Colorado to take steps to enable independent repair such that these copyright issues (including anticircumvention) never arise. This became the template for a slew of state repair bills, including Oregon's electronics repair law, which was later copy/pasted into Washington state law: https://pirg.org/oregon/updates/governor-kotek-signs-the-right-to-repair-act-into-law/ A very similar law was passed in New York state, only to be gutted by Governor Kathy Hochul: https://www.techdirt.com/2024/02/07/nys-right-to-repair-law-was-neutered-by-lobbyists-and-governor-hochul-after-passage-now-some-lawmakers-are-trying-to-fix-it/ Hochul will shortly get a chance to redeem herself, when A8405, a law that re-inserts all the provisions she stripped out of the original repair law, comes to her desk: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/A8405 Perhaps Hochul will sign that law. After all, her press release about the new automotive bill sure makes it sound like she's anti-enshittification: My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets. https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/money-your-pockets-governor-hochul-signs-bill-restricting-exploitative-vehicle-subscription But the specifics of this new NY automotive bill matter, and they're a decidedly mixed bag. Let's start with the penalty for noncompliance: a dealer, automotive manufacturer or lender who violates the new law faces a whopping $250 fine per violation. That means that if your dealer charges you $1,000 for a software upgrade and you later realize you've been ripped off, they'll only pay a penalty of $250. In this case, a dealer who manages to fleece one driver for every three who know their rights and can figure out how to enforce them will still come out ahead – and that's only if you can get the dealer to refund your $1000, which might involve going to small claims court. Then there's the carve-outs: this law does not cover subscription fees and software upsells for "navigation system updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle wi-fi, telematics services, roadside assistance, software-dependent driver assistance or driver automation features, or vehicle-connected services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This is a huge loophole. Take that last clause, "services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This clause allows manufacturers to bypass the entire statute, merely by redesigning their subscription and software upsells to "rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." For example, the BMW feature that automatically dips your high-beams could "require" a daily check for new versions and then the company can claim that the feature relies "on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." Sure, a judge might eventually find that "continued operation" doesn't mean a daily check for software updates, but only after the state AG or a class action lawyer forces the question, which could take years. Also: don't hold your breath waiting for the class action lawyer, because the car manufacturers can also make you click through a binding arbitration waiver when you first turn on your car and thus take away your right to join a class action: https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/27/shit-shack/#binding-arbitration Beyond this, there's the breadth of vague phrases like "driver automation features" (is automatically dipping your high-beams a "driver automation feature?" I could sure see a lawyer making that argument). Likewise "telematics" (a buzzword that might mean anything, nothing or everything). On the other hand, there are some interesting ambiguities in this bill that I quite like. For example: if you live in New Jersey, but you happen to be in New York on the day Tesla bills you for subscribing to your whole battery (some Tesla models only let you use half your battery's charge unless you pay a monthly fee). Does that mean Tesla violated the law by charging a fee for a subscription feature for a car that is in the state of New York? That would be a fun one to see! Like I said, this is only a partial fix for auto-enshittification. It won't stop your car from spying on you and ratting you out to your insurer: https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars It won't help you if the manufacturer goes bust and bricks your car: https://pluralistic.net/2024/10/10/software-based-car/#based It won't help you if Tesla hacks your odometer to sell a lie about the range you can expect from your charge: https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/28/edison-not-tesla/#demon-haunted-world This law would have had much more effect if it was better-drafted; on the other hand, maybe if it was drafted to capture a more meaningful slice of enshittificatory gambits, Hochul would have gutted it the way she did with the state's 2022 electronics repair bill. Above all, though, we must remember: the only reason this bill exists at all is that Congress created DMCA 1201, the "felony contempt of business-model" law that lets companies conjure new crimes out of thin air and send you to prison for making their shareholders sad. It's fantastic that the Repair Coalition came up with a loophole that lets states protect the American public from some of the worst effects of anticircumvention law, and it's cool that this tactic is being used to fight other kinds of enshittification. But none of this should be necessary at all, and the real fix is for Congress to repeal Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. item.title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
item.description:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027. EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users. What California’s Rules Say Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709. For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking. At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users. What New York’s Rules Say Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service. As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics. The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)). Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week. What This Means for Users in NY and CA Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today. When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights. At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine. Help Us Help You Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org. Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts. If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

Source feed: https://www.eff.org/rss/updates.xml

item.title: Pluralistic: Free lunches (24 Nov 2026)
item.description: Today's links Free lunches: Tech's margin is everyone else's opportunity. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Hacker v conman (twice); NESPaul; Record industry v DRM; 21 lb cherpumple; The rich don't "earn" their fortunes; Newscorp offers favorable personal coverage for senate votes; UC Davis x pepper spray; Was the Wisconsin vote hacked?; Definitively modeling distributional outcomes in Disney queuing systems. Upcoming appearances: Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Free lunches (permalink) An old joke: "Two economists are walking down the sidewalk and one of them points and says, 'Look, there's a $20 bill, right there on the ground!' The other one is dismissive: 'No, if that was a real $20, someone would have picked it up by now.'" If that joke leaves you scratching your head, then you've been lucky enough to avoid the neoclassical economist's view of the world as a market whose participants, in aggregate, know everything about what people are buying and selling. In that world if there's a "free lunch" &#8211; like a $20 bill on the sidewalk &#8211; someone will have already taken it. Likewise, if there's a seller who's priced their goods at $10 and a buyer who's willing to pay $30, there will be an "arbitrageur" who will be shuttling those $10 goods to those $30 customers and pocketing the difference. Give it enough time and either the seller will raise their price to $30, or the buyer will realize they should only be offering $10. The market will "clear," with everyone getting everything they need in the most efficient way possible, meaning there's no way to improve anyone's position without making someone else worse off: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency When markets don't behave like this, neoclassicals hunt for "distortions" that prevent the market from performing this continuous balancing trick. "Distortion" is best understood here as a euphemism for "democratic intervention." If you've ever gotten excited about a commonsense policy solution to a serious economic problem (like public grocery stores as a means of addressing food deserts and greedflation), only to see it shot down by economists who use a lot of jargon to "prove" that it can't possibly work, you've experienced how well "distortion" doomerism keeps us from having nice things. The economist's allergy to distortions is curiously selective. When a company uses its monopoly power to capture its regulators, or bind its workers to silence, or to erect barriers to entry that keep competitors at bay, somehow that doesn't qualify as a "distortion." Same goes for the situation in which a dominant retailer (Walmart) and a dominant manufacturer (Pepsi) come to a secret agreement to force everyone else to raise prices a ton so that Walmart can raise its prices by a (smaller) ton and still be "the cheapest": https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities Economists are in love with the idea of the economy as a self-licking ice-cream cone, a beautiful machine that operates all by itself, processing all the information we inject into it by buying and selling and finding the optimal way to produce more of the things we want best at the lowest prices. But like any love-drunk suitor, economists habitually overlook the market's glaring imperfections. In the self-correcting market, a company with high margins sends up a flare that alerts other, hungrier companies to swarm it, competing to offer the cheapest price. Likewise any company with lots of customers: those crowds of customers should conjure up armies of clever planners and inventors who find more efficient ways to produce the same goods and services and lure those customers away. This is the crux of market orthodoxy, the idea that competition lowers margins, goading sellers to offer better goods at better prices. Don't take my word for it, here's Adam Smith: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages. If this is true, then the surest sign of a "market distortion" is persistent high margins and persistent high market-share. Any company that dominates its market and charges far more than its costs is a crisp, $20 bill lying right there on the sidewalk for all to see. If no one picks up that $20, then it's a sure bet that there's a "distorter" who is preventing the market from acting on the "information" that there is an opportunity here. America's business lobby loves distortions, so long as they're the kinds of distortions that let the companies safely entrust their $20 bills to the sidewalk without worrying about having them scooped up by a competitor. Take Big Tech: this is an industry with such persistently high margins and so many customers that there are multiple firms in the sector that were able to piss away hundreds of billions of dollars by manipulating their stock prices with buybacks and building AI data-centers that can never turn a profit: https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs If the market was "undistorted" then anyone this rich and this stupid would be in serious trouble. Ask a neoclassical to explain Big Tech's prolonged, morbid wealth and they'll insist that this means that we're the stupid ones, because we can't play 11-dimensional chess like Zuckerberg, which is why we can't understand why it was good to piss away $80b on the metaverse. But we don't have to look very hard to find another, simpler explanation. Big Tech owes its profits to its monopoly power, which allows it to form cartels that collude to rig prices: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue Big Tech has so much money that it can capture its regulators, securing favorable laws that make it literally illegal to build competing products, so we're all stuck as hostages of the platforms: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/14/sole-and-despotic/#world-turned-upside-down An "undistorted" market is one where information is presumed to flow freely among market participants. But the business lobby has secured far-reaching legal protection for the nondisclosure and noncompete "agreements" it crams down the throats of its workers, customers and suppliers, making it literally illegal to warn other people about the defects in both its products and its managers' character: https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/27/zuckerstreisand-2/#autodisparagement An "undistorted" market is one in which the state intervenes to enforce contracts. Without that intervention, cheaters can beat trustworthy competitors by making promises they have no intention of keeping. Yet, the business lobby has secured government backing for "binding arbitration" waivers that make it illegal to sue people who cheat you, forcing you to have your case heard by a fake judge who works for the cheater and nearly always rules in their favor (and whose rulings are legally secret, so you can't warn others so they don't get cheated as well): https://pluralistic.net/2020/04/11/socialized-losses/#justice-restored "Undistorted" markets are supposed to keep firms lean and energetic, forever on the lookout for new ways to attract the best customers and the best workers with the best deals and the best pay. Decades of lax merger enforcement has produced an economy dominated by fat and lazy cartels who substitute bullying and lock-in for innovation and customer service: https://www.openmarketsinstitute.org/learn/monopoly-by-the-numbers The business lobby and their tame economists have invented all kinds of gimmicks to "disprove" your intuition that you're worse off every year thanks to cheaters and their rising profits. For example, there are plenty of mainstream economists who insist that the wage stagnation that has trapped American workers for decades is a hoax. They point to statistics that show that when you include "transfers," American workers are doing just as well as their foreign counterparts, and in particular, that the American public continues to enjoy healthy levels of "consumption" (buying things). These are very dodgy stats indeed. Here's how they're calculated: the American consumption figures include the health care received by the American public. That health care includes Medicare payments on behalf of Americans who age out of employer-provided insurance, and Medicaid payments made on behalf of poor Americans. These medical services cost 200-300% more than the same services when provided in other advanced economies (Canada, Germany, the UK, etc). So when a poor American in Buffalo gets Medicaid dialysis at three times the price of a dialysis session in Toronto, that is counted toward that poor person's consumption levels, as though they had just gone out and spent hundreds of dollars on treats from the Cheesecake Factory and the Apple Store. In reality, they've received an overpriced service (whose costs were absorbed by the public purse). They haven't seen an extra dime to spend on either the necessities of life or a little treat: https://capitalisnt.com/episodes/can-capitalism-be-popular-FcXPThM6 America spends more on health-care than any other rich nation, and gets less for its money than anyone else. In other words: neoclassical economists use the sky-high monopoly prices set by America's overpriced, underdelivering health care cartel to claim that we've got tons of "real" income, because they factor in the hundreds of billions in public subsidy the feds and the states funnel to these persistently high-margin (and therefore definitively inefficient) businesses. Get rid of the statistical mirages and a very different America comes into focus: one in which large businesses have fused with a corrupted state that serves as bagman and enforcer for the corporate sector as it rips off workers and consumers. Remember the decades when tech bros insisted that their "disruption" was all in service to shattering the death grip that legacy industries had on our economy? Uber's early champions insisted that the taxi sector had been "distorted" by overreaching regulation. Once Uber injected "information" about willing riders and willing drivers into the system, the market would clear, pairing drivers and riders in such a way that no one could be made better off without making someone else worse off. Today, Uber uses its lock-in to pay drivers less and less and charge riders more and more &#8211; and Uber uses IP law to prevent competitors from making an app that lets drivers automatically shop for better pay and apps that let riders find cheaper rides: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/11/your-risk/#my-reward Uber's "perfect market" is a government-backed monopoly, reliant on the state to block anyone from reverse-engineering its app or unionizing its workers. That fusion of the corporation and the state funnels billions from drivers and riders to investors. Amazon's founding principle is best summed up in Jeff Bezos's oft-repeated motto, "Your margin is my opportunity." Today, 51-60% of every sale on Amazon's platform is captured by the platform. AWS, Amazon's cloud service, is no longer its most profitable line of business. Today, Amazon's largest source of profit is the $80b it makes every year from charging for search-placement, extracting bribes from sellers to show you items that cost more than the best match for your query: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/04/cheating-at-fraud/#absentee-rentier That's a lot of margin &#8211; and a lot of opportunity. Same goes for Apple: the company's most profitable line of business is the 30% app tax it levies on every payment made using an iPhone or iPad. Apple makes $100b/year charging a 30% commission on payments that cost the company less than 1% to process. That's a lot of margin. Then there's the ad-tech duopoly, Meta/Google. These two companies make so much money in an ad system where they represent both buyers and sellers in marketplaces they operate (where they also buy and sell), that they have hundreds of billions left to blow on AI misadventures: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/19/spying-v-context/#unattributed In other words, Big Tech's sidewalk is covered in $20 bills, which the US government bans American firms from picking up. But that's America. What about the rest of the world? Well, for 25 years, the US Trade Representative has made it America's business to see to it that every US trading partner enacted laws that protected America's tech companies from competitors. Thus the UK's pavements are littered with 20 pound notes, and the EU's are covered in 20 euro notes: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition The US Trade Rep used both a carrot and a stick to extract these policy concessions from the rest of the world. The carrot was the promise of tariff-free access to the American consumer (the world's richest, shoppingest, most numerous consumer cohort) &#8211; the stick was the threat of tariffs. Today, the stick is broken and the carrot is gone. The American consumer's wallet has been drained. American homeowners groan under multiple mortgages. American renters give 50% of their paycheck to Wall Street slumlords. The US healthcare system has emptied their bank accounts and student debt came for the rest. When American economists have to use the fact that you're too poor to afford overpriced health-care to "prove" that you're rolling in dough, you know the end is nigh. America's growth industries are "financial services" that let you pay for a burrito in four installments &#8211; and gambling. The median American worker has $955 saved for retirement: https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/12/always-great/#our-nhs Then there's tariffs: as November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor and flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play." The tariffs Trump imposed on every country in the world (even the uninhabited penguin islands) destroyed tariffs' deterrent value: https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations America's tech margins are the world's opportunity. It's time to move fast and break (tech's) things. It's time to move fast and break kings. Any economist who truly believes in markets would cheer this on: after all, repealing the "market-distorting" laws the US bound the world to can only increase market efficiency, right? Get rid of trade secrecy, nondisclosure and nondisparagement so that market actors have the information they need to make buy/sell decisions. Get rid of IP laws that block reverse-engineering, scraping and other tactics that facilitate switching to a competitor's service, using your own payment processor, or hijacking and rewriting search results to purge paid placement. Silicon Valley told us we all have a duty to disrupt sclerotic, top-heavy, lazy industries and treat their margins as our opportunity. When they did it to us, that wasn't progress. If we do it to them, that's not piracy. It's just business. item.title: Pluralistic: The Debt Trap (23 Nov 2026)
item.description: Today's links The Debt Trap: Obscure causality is the downfall of us all. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: They Fight Crime; Cantenna wifi TV for Mali; Kakistocracy; Inflation or price-gouging; The long game; Fox v bloggers; Hollywood laundered money for Berlusoni; Katamari earmuffs; EMI v parody cricket songs; "Roller Girl"; Trump U was worse than you thought; London v Dieselgate; Bunnie at USC; Facebook gaslights the web; Apple bans ebooks that mention Apple; Private ambulances v babies in burning buildings; Boss preppers. Upcoming appearances: Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. The Debt Trap (permalink) Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free): https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects: https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/ I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say definitively that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but why was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is hard, especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death. The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic because it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate. What's more, it's this same attenuated causality (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, some of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able (is able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff. I believe that most of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect. This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence. For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts &#8211; to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses &#8211; after the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon. This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact good policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs. Thus Biden's initial proposal: let Medicare/Medicaid negotiate drug prices the same way every private insurer and every public health system does. But then, Biden's team allowed that policy to be diluted so that it would only apply to ten drugs, and only if those drugs had been on the market for at least 13 years. Finally, the piece de resistance: the plan wasn't design to kick in until 2025, after the 2024 election, which turned out to be a referendum on the cost of living (including drug prices) that saw the Dems getting their asses kicked by the stupidest, most obviously corrupt fascists in American electoral history: https://pluralistic.net/2021/11/18/bipartisan-consensus/#corruption Whether you're ignoring attenuated causality or weaponizing it, it's critical to any analysis of how we get into as much trouble as we do. It is the ruin of individuals and firms, and of political and economic systems. Take vaccinations: herd immunity requires a lot of compliance: nearly all of us have to get vaccinated before the real benefits kick in. Securing this compliance takes a lot of effort, because the system has to get people to invest their faith in the prospect that eventually we'll get to herd immunity and an end to infection. But once herd immunity is in place, noncompliance is a much smaller deal. The very fact of herd immunity means that people can opt out here or there without getting sick (because we're all up-to-date on our vaccinations). Worse, the very fact of herd immunity means that after a while, no one can really remember what the sickness was like: we think of measles as something the Little Rascals pretended to have so they could play hooky, not as a terrifyingly infectious disease that can leave you blind or brain damaged. Asking someone who's never lived through a measles epidemic to estimate the cost of measles is like asking a 13 year old to estimate what a cancer diagnosis will feel like. The same applies to antitrust enforcement. An economy of small and medium sized firms who compete with one another is an economy where workers have more bargaining leverage and regulators don't have to worry about being outspent and outlasted with decade-plus appeals when they crack down on corrupt businesses: https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/15/business/us-vsibm.html It's also an economy where companies must compete rather than collude. Look at what happened to the ad-tech industry, which is dominated by a duopoly that controls 80% of display advertising, and that duopoly has an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the market to pay publishers less and charge advertisers more: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue In the post-war era, antitrust enforcers did their jobs: they blocked mergers, punished predatory pricing, and aggressively investigated sweetheart deals between retail incumbents and their suppliers that were designed to freeze out new businesses: https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities This produced an economy where companies had lower profits, because workers and consumers could force them to disgorge more of their surpluses, and because they had to invest more in improving their offerings to keep up with competitors. It was an economy where prosperity was more broadly shared and where it was easier to impose democratic accountability on the private sector. Then, starting with Jimmy Carter, America turned its back on antitrust. Year after year, presidency after presidency, enforcers waved through larger and more anticompetitive mergers and ignored more egregious predatory practices. For 50 years, the neoclassical economists who promoted this laissez-faire doctrine have smugly pointed out that even though the economy grew more consolidated thanks to their policy, we still had an economy, one that was often booming, where politicians could (sometimes) be seen to be intervening to address corporate cheating. The public, meanwhile, has historically struggled to connect the problems of oligarchy with these pro-oligarch policies. They can feel the regulatory capture, they know that labor grows weaker every year, they are furious at their sellout politicians and the system's naked corruption. But because the policy is separated from its outcomes by so much time and space, there's lots of room for the policy's architects and beneficiaries to do the economic version of denying the link between smoking and cancer; that is, denying the link between pro-monopoly policies and monopolies. Attenuated causality lets bad-faith actors sell us anti-vax, pro-monopoly, cancer denial&#8230;and, of course, climate denial. NASA's James Hansen warned Congress about climate change in 1988. It's not like the oil companies didn't know about this. As far back as the 1970s, Exxon's own scientists had warned the company about global warming, and the company took actions based on those warnings: https://insideclimatenews.org/project/exxon-the-road-not-taken/ Mobil, meanwhile, started secretly raising its drilling platforms to account for rising seas, even as it was taking out full-page ads in national daily newspapers that stated that "The science of climate change is too uncertain to mandate a plan of action": https://web.archive.org/web/20160101024248/http://graphics.latimes.com/oil-operations/ Attenuated causality was and is at the core of climate denial. If every climate-shredding gas turbine that the self-described environmental hero Elon Musk fired up at one of his AI data-centers immediately caused a flood or a wildfire or a heat-wave, we'd scrape all those data-centers down to their foundation slabs and then we'd display Musk in stocks and pelt him with rotten fruit. Musk really knows how to turn attenuated causality to his advantage. Remember when he performatively borrowed a security guard's pocket knife and started slicing through the Ethernet cables connecting Twitter's servers? https://english.elpais.com/science-tech/2023-09-14/when-elon-musk-unplugged-the-twitter-servers-with-a-pocket-knife-theres-still-shit-thats-broken-because-of-it.html Or when he started shutting down whole data-centers and mass-firing Twitter's technical staff? https://www.nytimes.com/2022/12/29/technology/twitter-elon-musk.html The point of this performance was to let Musk claim that Twitter's management had let itself be gulled by featherbedding engineers who grossly overbuilt Twitter's infrastructure in order to guarantee themselves perpetual employment at the expense of Twitter's shareholders. But all that spare server capacity wasn't excess: it was the cushion, the headroom, the insurance policy. Those were the servers that would pick up the slack when another server lost its power-supply or caught a bad stick of RAM. They were the servers that could shoulder the load during the next 9/11 or Arab Spring. They were the engineering staff that could execute new projects or perform emergency maintenance &#8211; and the engineering staff that could plan the next build-out in advance so that future growth wouldn't stall out when Twitter ran out of hardware. Musk's actions didn't occur in a vacuum. During the decades in which attenuated causality set the scene for an endless, incestuous orgy of mergers and acquisitions, it became normal for business leaders to hack away at their own firms' resiliency. University administrators fired tenured professors and replaced them with casualized, proletarianized adjuncts. The pedagogy &#8211; and the universities' reputations &#8211; persisted after the cuts, ebbing away slowly as the institutional memory and standards eroded bit by bit. But eventually, the universities found themselves in crisis. Campuses erupted in student revolt and spectacular scenes of violent repression: https://jayrosen.tumblr.com/post/13174138991/excerpt-from-uc-davis-2010-2012-general-catalog Universities' reputations cratered and they found themselves easy pickings for demagogues who awarded themselves a veto over faculty, curriculum and admissions: https://www.chronicle.com/article/columbia-capitulated-but-so-did-the-rest-of-higher-ed That's the thing about attenuated causality: it lets people and institutions and systems play a high-stakes game of Jenga in which every non-load-bearing block is removed and added to the top of the teetering stack. No one block causes the system to collapse&#8230;until one block does, and the whole thing falls over. It's like an avalanche. Drop one snowflake after another on the mountainside. Expose it to the midday sun and the frigid night. Sure, it creaks. Watch closely and you'll see it make minute shifts. Every now and again, a light scree of snow slides off the surface and skitters downhill, but the great mass of snow is stable. Until it isn't. Until one last snowflake alights on the mountainside and sets the whole thing rumbling and tumbling in an inexorable, unstoppable wall of snow that only halts when it can go no lower. The run-up to an avalanche is a long, long series of linear phenomena. A snowflake is minute. Add it to the pile and it will produce a minute effect. A little bit of heat causes a little bit of expansion. A little bit of wind blows a little of the loose cover around. But each one of these little strains on the system makes it less stable overall. The snowpack's stability is invisible. A snowpack that is about to cut loose is indistinguishable from one that will stay put for weeks or months. But once the snow's systemic resiliency has been exhausted, the next linear perturbation produces a wild, catastrophic, nonlinear collapse. Attenuated causality lets us build up a mountain of debt: health debt, technology debt, policy debt, credibility debt. It's impossible to know when the system's homeostatic mechanisms have been fatally weakened, such that the next compromise it is asked to bear causes it to rupture, or implode, or crumble. We can raise the level of CO2 and methane in the Earth's atmosphere year after year and see long-attenuated, linear effects: fires here, floods there, some extinctions. But one day: we overwhelm some invisible homeostatic mechanism and we lose the Gulf Stream: https://www.bbc.com/climate/impact/gulf_stream.shtml Same goes for the world's IT: we can fire IT workers, starve maintenance teams of budget and personnel, substitute indemnity for software quality, allow our "security" agencies to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities, and on average, it will all work&#8230;until it stops: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake IT might just be the most dangerously attenuated aspect of all our administrative functions. A software engineer writes a piece of code and it keeps running, even if you fire that engineer. This is one of the reasons it's so hard to unionize tech workers: when they go on strike, their scab software crosses the picket line and keeps working: https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/07/aeiou-but-sometimes-why/#unrecognizable-playbook But software isn't an asset, it's a liability. Code runs in a system, with upstream processes that produce its inputs and downstream processes that operate on its outputs. There's adjacent processes, too: other software that also gets fed by those upstream processes and also feeds those downstream processes. Even if the code never changes, the system the code is part of changes constantly, which means that the more code you have, the more code you have to maintain. So what happens when you fire technical workers is nothing&#8230;at first. And then, bit by bit, things start to break. And break. And break. Only the people who wrote the software &#8211; and the people they trained through working alongside of them &#8211; know exactly how it works, with that deep knowledge, that Fingerspitzengefühl, that informs their intuition so they can figure out why things broke and how to fix them: https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/08/process-knowledge/#dance-monkey-dance Break that chain of knowledge and you lobotomize your institution. Reduce the full complement of experienced engineers with the wherewithal to demand higher wages and better conditions, leave behind a precarious skeleton crew of juniors you terrorize with layoff threats and AI ghost-stories, and you destroy not just your ability to spot problems before they occur, but also your capability to salvage your way out of the wreckage. And that's what Musk's Doge did to the American state: undermined its capacity to absorb shocks, to anticipate shocks and brace for them &#8211; or even to detect the shocks when they're underway. There's a reason so much variation is preserved in our genomes and species: these are the reserves of variety that can rise to meet the changing world. item.title: EFF to Congress: Mass Surveillance Is Too Important to Shove into Must-Pass Bill
item.description:
In June 2026, the surveillance authority Section 702 of FISA expired absent a consensus among lawmakers over the terms of its reauthorization. Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a letter with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill. The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. It should not be used as a vehicle to circumvent or to cut short this long-running bipartisan debate over Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, nor to force lawmakers to choose between supporting our national defense and ending warrantless spying on Americans. Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process.” You can read the entire letter here. Section 702 grants the government authority to compel a telecommunications company to hand over data to the National Security Agency (NSA) in an attempt to protect national security by monitoring communications overseas—but this is only a piece of what the law does. Because we live in a globalized world, communications between people in other countries and in the United States often gets hoovered up. Once it does, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and several other agencies give themselves permission to search through U.S. persons’ data without a warrant. This is unconstitutional, undermines our right to private communications, and creates a dangerous and potent tool for would-be despots who might use that communication to discriminate, marginalize, or punish people based on their identities and political beliefs. This is not the kind of policy Congress should be considering without necessary reforms, open debate, and the ability for lawmakers to vote against without forcing them to vote “no” on all defense policy. We once again urge Congress not to put Section 702’s future in a must-pass bill like the NDAA.

Source feed: https://www.eff.org/rss/updates.xml

item.title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
item.description:
Nvidia's board is now coming under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty ImagesThe story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO, Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions, it’s even more difficult. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks. Another issue is moral hazard: when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. CHIP SOMODEVILLA/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted: “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.” Michael Nalick does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

Source feed: https://theconversation.com/us/technology/articles.atom

item.title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
item.description:
Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements. Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft, Apple*, banks, courts, airlines, and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally. There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug, negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur. In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail. The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital. The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures, one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. Even if you see the problem coming, an outage that hits clients, suppliers, collaborators or loved ones proves just as disruptive. We need to remove these chokepoints for good, which means a digital sovereignty movement that makes the web more free by design—not just importing existing levers of control into another nation's borders. Central to this effort must be undercutting platform control by fostering interoperability, i.e. when tools are made to be compatible among competitors. When this is done carefully, it’s not only easier to switch to better alternatives, we wind up with more alternatives as it becomes more viable to compete or offer complementary tools alongside existing systems. This is what made systems like email great. You could choose your own apps and services, even using several simultaneously, and never lose touch with a contact. Early architects of the internet did not take reliable hosting for granted. Services were often on a machine a few rooms over, and needed to be prepared for the occasional interruption of service. But in the age of hyperscalers and massive data centers, the infrastructure underlying the web isn’t owned by many scattered IT departments, it’s rented from a handful of “cloud” providers. These providers managed to scale up quickly and replace interoperability with walled gardens, enticing customers with lower costs while making it costly to leave and tightly controlling how services behave. Once in control, these platforms have every incentive to enshittify their services and devalue their workers, delivering an increasingly shoddy and restrictive service. This context makes building interoperability an act of defiance—often coming from the sweat of open source developers. These projects may be tolerated by monopolists in the short term, but can be one boardroom decision away from being broken entirely. A better internet means championing these creators through funding, liability protections, and requiring big players to cooperate. Here is what lawmakers should do: Federal and state legislators should— Defend competitive compatibility. Developers merely providing alternative interfaces for tools should be shielded from liability. In the U.S., that means explicit protections under DMCA, CFAA, and corporate Terms of Service agreements. These protections should cover shared protocols and APIs as well as automated content retrieval through scraping. Encourage interoperability. Lawmakers should force open key aspects of platform infrastructure by requiring big tech to support: (1) data portability, so users can move to a new service (2) back-end interoperability, to support more tools with competitive compatibility and (3) delegability, so people are not prevented from having code act on their behalf. So far, the Digital Markets Act in the EU has provided some positive examples of such legislation Fund open source. In order to be sustainable, interoperable tools and standards cannot rely solely on corporate interest and volunteer labor. Programs like the EU Sovereign Tech Fund could help create viable alternatives within and beyond the borders of the EU. Municipalities and institutions should— Buy interoperable services. At any level, government agencies should set minimum interoperability requirements in procurement and hold a competitive bidding process to evaluate vendors’ privacy, security and lock-in risks. Agencies dependent on a sole provider, including through cooperative purchase agreements, are stuck with corporate price-gouging and even higher switching costs. Fund Departments of Information Technology. Cloud services are often adopted to offset spending on IT professionals but, when these departments atrophy, institutions become even more reliant on the cloud providers. Maintaining in-house talent prevents this cycle of dependency and improves emergency responses to outages. Adopt a plus-one approach to public communications. Institutions shouldn’t force citizens into walled gardens just to access public communications. In addition to posts to corporate social media, government agencies should share the same information on an open protocol—whether it’s bluesky, the fediverse, or just an RSS feed. By putting these in the open, more people will have access to urgent alerts and can create new useful tools. Building a more resilient and democratic internet is possible, and many people are already hard at work doing just that. Above are some necessary steps to get corporate and government interests out of the way of rewilding the net with greater community and individual controls. The dream of the internet as a digital commons operating for the public good is not dead yet, and is worth fighting for. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

item.title: Surveillance Isn't Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
item.description:
In the new comic "Surveillance Isn't Safety"—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It's a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs). Jump to the Comic Or download the PDF Published in collaboration between EFF and Crucial Comix, Bryn's comic captures the authenticity of the grassroot backlash against the surveillance industry—undercutting Flock founder Garrett Langley's latest dubious defense that public opposition of his company's product isn't real. At the International Association of Chiefs of Police conference this fall, Langley accused the anti-surveillance activism of being driven by Russian bots and as being "inorganic." He pointed to the fact that many local groups were using similar language in their protest signs as supposed proof, when in reality, shared slogans are one of the hallmarks of a social movement. This was all misdirection from the grim realities that Flock and other ALPR systems facilitate: the mistakes are real; the abuse is real; the racism is real; and the targeting of dissenters, migrants, and abortion seekers is real. And, importantly, the cancelled contracts are real. Bryn's comic sheds light on the real abuses and threats driving communities to mobilize against Flock, Axon, and other ALPR vendors. It shows that coast-to-coast activism doesn't happen overnight—any more than a comic appears out of thin air as a finished product. As advisors on the cartoon, EFF watched how Bryn's script evolved from rough sketches to penciled drawings, then to inked and shaded panels, mirroring how the long-running movement against mass surveillance has steadily snowballed over the last few years. There is nothing “inorganic” about either: Both are built on passion, commitment, and putting in the work. Surveillance Isn't Safety Joining the fight against Flock and other foes Author: Bryn Adams, Editors: Shay Mirk (Crucial Comix) and Dave Maass (EFF) This comic is jointly published by Crucial Comix and the Electronic Frontier Foundation.
