item.title: Voters Reject ALPRs and Surveillance Tech at the Ballot Box
item.description:
Do automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities? That question has been a hot topic in city council meetings, community conversations, and news coverage around the country for months. This past election day, a couple U.S communities took it further: to the ballot. And overwhelmingly, voters decided that, no, these devices should not be deployed on our streets. We agree! In Maine, the coastal community of York voted to remove the town’s existing ALPR cameras and require that any future proposed installations receive voter approval before proceeding. The local initiative ended up on the ballot after constituents gathered enough signatures on a citizens’ petition for a local ordinance. On Election Day, nearly three-quarters of York voters supported the ban. Thousands of miles away, voters in League City, Texas also voted against allowing the local police department to continue use of ALPR cameras. That vote was formally approved on November 17, which began a 72-hour window to remove the cameras. Since the election, the cameras have been “bagged” or covered to prevent the collection of data. At least one city also decided to expand protections afforded to their residents when it comes to the use of surveillance technology. In Pflugerville, Texas, Proposition B passed, now requiring that the City Charter be amended to include “protections governing the collection, use, retention, and oversight of data, facial recognition, and surveillance technologies.” It also requires “a responsible artificial intelligence framework.” While every municipality has different rules for how to get a local ordinance placed on the ballot, banning use and securing the removal of surveillance tools locally is a powerful way of protecting your community against devices and data collection that goes far beyond your town lines. Surveillance is a choice, not a mandate, and our communities have the power to refuse it. EFF has supported local communities around the country over the last few years in advocating against the procurement of surveillance technologies in their cities, counties, and states. These victories at the ballot box and in city councils show that when mass surveillance is presented as a policy choice, not a technical necessity, communities can and do reject it. Do you know what surveillance tools are being used by your local police departments? Check out the Atlas of Surveillance to learn more about the tools in your city, and sign up to volunteer if you want to push for more transparency across the country.

item.title: The Justice Department Wants To Give Patent Trolls More Power
item.description:
Software patents are mostly vague, hard to define, and widely abused. Most tech patent lawsuits aren’t filed by companies that make real products. They’re filed by patent trolls, companies that acquire patents to extract payments through litigation and legal threats. A patent on one feature of a smartphone shouldn’t give the patent owner the power to threaten the existence of the entire product line. But that is exactly the leverage patent trolls want—and the current administration is helping them to get it. In two recent patent cases, Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung and Collision Communications v. Samsung, the Justice Department and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have asked courts to make it easier for patent owners to get injunctions. These are judicial orders that can force companies to stop selling products or remove features from them, rather than simply pay monetary damages. The threat of an injunction can pressure a company to pay far more than what a patent is actually worth. In 2006, NTP Inc., a patent holding company with no products of its own, was able to pressure BlackBerry manufacturer Research in Motion Ltd. to pay a $612 million settlement when it was on the verge of an injunction. Protection Against Patent Trolls In May 2006, the Supreme Court rejected the practice of granting permanent injunctions almost automatically after a finding of patent infringement. In eBay v. MercExchange, the high court held that patent owners must satisfy the same tough requirements that plaintiffs in non-patent cases must meet to get a permanent injunction. After eBay, patent owners had to show “irreparable harm,” that they can’t be adequately compensated by money, that the “balance of hardships” favors the plaintiff, and, critically, that an injunction would not harm the “public interest.” At EFF, we celebrated eBay v. MercExchange as a major win for internet users. More than twenty years ago, we saw that software patents were going to be a disaster—not just for small companies (which they are), but for freedom of expression online. As EFF explained in its brief: The United States Patent and Trademark Office has issued patents on methods fordownloading video programs, publishing web pages, sending email messages, making internet telephone calls, and even online fundraising methods. Injunctions against uses of these technologies—and many similar technologies—will inevitably affect, and may even chill, free expression on the internet. The eBay rules make sense because the monopolies provided by patents are only justified when they serve a public purpose: promoting scientific and technological progress. Enforcing patents is not supposed to come at the cost of later innovators, free expression, or people’s access to technology. Now, two decades after eBay, the government is urging courts to interpret those protections in ways that could give patent owners greater leverage. It’s unusual for the government to intervene in private patent disputes, but the current administration has done so repeatedly—and not on the side of the public. Patent Licensing Disputes Shouldn't Threaten Entire Product Lines In June 2025, the Justice Department and Patent Office filed a “statement of interest” in Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung, a dispute over patents involving solid-state drives (SSDs), the storage devices commonly used in modern computers. Radian, a patent assertion company tied to Fortress Investment Group, sought a preliminary injunction that would block sales of Samsung’s products even before a judge or jury had decided whether there was patent infringement. In its statement, the government argued that even a patent owner whose business depends entirely on patent licensing could suffer irreparable harm, because calculating how much money it should get might be difficult. “In cases of unique assets, courts have commonly found irreparable harm when damages are difficult to calculate,” the DOJ writes in its brief. But courts regularly resolve disagreements about patent royalty rates, a patent’s contribution, and comparable licenses. The fact that those disagreements exist does not, by itself, establish that monetary damages wouldn’t be enough to compensate the patent owner. If courts adopted the DOJ’s views here, a difficult but ordinary part of patent litigation could become a reason for finding irreparable harm, making it easier for patent owners to seek injunctions that threaten entire product lines. Pure patent-licensing businesses would love that—they would routinely start to ask for injunctions, since eBay’s most important protections would be weakened. The government also says that “the prospect of an injunction can facilitate negotiation among the parties.” That’s exactly the problem. A company negotiating under threat of shutdown might pay massive sums to patent litigation shops in order to avoid disruption to product lines or customers. The payment is more likely to reflect the value of the threat, rather than the value of a patent. Radian ultimately withdrew its request for a preliminary injunction, but the government's arguments about when injunctions should be available remain concerning. A Second Attempt To Weaken eBay Remarkably, the government returned to this argument in February of this year, in a case called Collision Communications v. Samsung, which had already gone to trial. In this case, Collision, a patent-licensing entity that acquired its patents from a defense contractor, was awarded a $445.5 million jury verdict for infringement of four patents, and then sought an injunction. Even though the jury had awarded Collision $445.5 million in damages, the government still intervened in the case, arguing that patent owners like Collision, which do not make products, should not be denied injunctions because they rely on patent licensing. They also argued that the difficulty of calculating monetary damages can support an injunction. Although the court agreed that Collision had suffered irreparable harm and that monetary damages would be inadequate, U.S. District Court Judge Rodney Gilstrap rejected Collision’s argument that ongoing patent infringement automatically establishes irreparable harm. He ultimately denied the injunction because Collision didn’t satisfy two other requirements of the eBay test: showing that the balance of hardships favored an injunction and that an injunction would not harm the public interest. Now Collision has appealed, and the argument is in front of the Federal Circuit, the nation’s top patent court. A brief from the Public Interest Patent Law Institute (PIPLI) explains what is at stake: when a patent owner doesn’t have any products, an injunction can prevent the public from accessing critical technology altogether. Since the patents here involve how mobile phones connect to cellular networks, “the effect on the public goes far beyond what these patents claim as improvements,” PIPLI explains. The outcome could extend well beyond these two companies. The eBay test requires courts to consider who a permanent injunction would hurt, and who would benefit—including the public. A patent owner’s desire for more negotiating leverage should not override the interests of millions of people who rely on their phones. Yet that’s exactly the kind of leverage the government’s arguments could make it easier for patent owners to obtain, at the expense of the public. The Government Should Protect the Public, Not Patent Owners Patent owners can already collect damages and royalties when their patents are infringed. But they should not get a shortcut to shutting down tech products just because calculating damages is hard work. The Justice Department should defend the eBay safeguard. Instead, this administration is helping patent owners find ways around it. Courts should reject those arguments. We shouldn’t even have to say it, but we do: making patent threats more valuable does not align with the public’s interest. This post is the second of a three-part series about how the current administration is using its power to give patent holders more power at the public’s expense. The final post will publish next week. See our previous post: How the USPTO is undermining patent reviews

item.title: The Paramount-Warner Brothers Deal Could Usher in Another Age of Lost Media
item.description:
There are all sorts of reasons to be against the merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers-Discovery. There's the obvious problem of increasing concentration in the already pretty-concentrated film and TV industry. People have problems with Paramount's owner Skydance interfering with its news coverage and late night comedy. But one of the biggest is the way we are losing choice and access to information and culture. In the context of the digital world, there are two major problems with these mega mergers. One, as we've said in the past, is that it further degrades the already awful state of mainstream streaming services. In short, by increasing the amount of legacy content under their control, major studios don't have to invest in either new content or well-engineered services to get users. Plus, they can pool the data they have on users together in an increasing assault on consumer privacy. A monthly subscription and more information about your habits and interests? Win-win for them. Another problem is the disappearing of content. In the digital era, there should be no more lost media. Making and storing copies of media is easier and cheaper than it ever has been. The idea of the persistence of content online has become the adage "the internet never forgets." However, since more and more media is locked behind subscription services under the control of fewer and fewer companies—and as physical copies, or even just digital copies that are actually owned by consumers also vanish—access to our common culture is at risk. Incentives to take information and media offline should raise huge red flags. Unfortunately, they are multiplying. First, there's the impulse of merged companies to offset the cost of their merger by shelving projects and claiming them as tax write-offs. We saw this the last time Warner Brothers was taken over, with projects being ended in order to take advantage of a specific kind of tax benefit. It has little to do with the quality or even how much or how complete a project is—money is the driving factor and we as a culture are all poorer for it. And we all know it. That's why the outrage eventually led to Coyote vs Acme being released by a much smaller studio. But not every project can count on having the perfect storm that brings a movie or show back from the dead. Second, there's the imposition of a new owner's own goals and beliefs upon its new acquisition. Some choices might seem kind of benign, like Discovery axing a lot of family-friendly and kid-oriented content from HBO Max. Of course, when one of the things affected is a pillar of childhood like Sesame Street, the loss of access to old episodes becomes a loss to the culture and not just a change in direction. Another area where we might lose access to information is in the radical shift in direction for news reporting. Reporters have resigned and more are being offered buy-outs to support the change in direction. Whether this will escalate to older projects being removed from streaming services or quietly buried in the recommendation algorithm is yet to be seen, but remains a real possibility. And it's not lost on anyone that one of the outlets reporting on the chaos at CBS News was CNN, which is now owned by the same people who own CBS News. The loss of diverse sources of news, as imperfect as we may have thought they were, hurts all of us. It makes it harder to access information and diverse points of view. Finally, media disappears as licenses expire and as studios decide they no longer want to pay residuals or backend deals to the creative people who made the work in the first place. Again, this looks like business decisions but if the works were exclusively available via streaming, those movies disappear forever. That both contributes to the idea that works are disposable and that paying the workers who made the art is not as important as shareholder value. On top of all of this, draconian copyright regimes and the anti-user product designs they create have made it nearly impossible for people to archive this material on their own—as many used to using VCRs. It’s easy to see a crisis in access to culture and information brewing, at the same time that it should be easier than ever to preserve and make available our shared digital culture.

item.title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: Snowden Exposes NSA’s Lies
item.description:
By 2013, EFF had spent seven years arguing in court that the National Security Agency was sweeping up ordinary Americans’ communications, including through the secret room that whistleblower Mark Klein had exposed. The government would neither confirm nor deny it, and outside the courtroom the public seemed to have moved on. Then, in early June, documentary filmmaker Laura Poitras and journalist Glenn Greenwald mysteriously missed a Freedom of the Press Foundation board meeting at EFF’s offices. It turned out they were in Hong Kong, meeting an NSA contractor who had been secretly writing to Laura for months. His name was Edward Snowden, he had thousands of secret documents proving the government had in fact been spying on millions of Americans. When he subsequently revealed himself, a photo of him sitting behind his laptop – emblazoned with a big red EFF sticker – went worldwide. Welcome to the fourth episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was. %3Ciframe%20height%3D%2252px%22%20width%3D%22100%25%22%20frameborder%3D%22no%22%20scrolling%3D%22no%22%20seamless%3D%22%22%20src%3D%22https%3A%2F%2Fplayer.simplecast.com%2F21ba982d-0892-47e9-a638-36b5fae0e2d7%3Fdark%3Dtrue%26amp%3Bcolor%3D000000%22%20allow%3D%22autoplay%22%3E%3C%2Fiframe%3E Privacy info. This embed will serve content from simplecast.com (You can also find this episode on the Internet Archive and on YouTube.) In this episode, former EFF Executive Director Cindy Cohn talks with Laura Poitras about how she got to that historic moment, including her years of expertise in communicating via encrypted channels. Freedom of the Press Foundation Executive Director Trevor Timm – a former EFF activist – shares his recollection of the day the first Snowden story broke. For EFF and its clients in Jewel v. NSA, Snowden’s documents were proof of what the government had spent years refusing to confirm. As Cindy puts it, “We were struggling along in the mud, and we felt like somebody gave us wings.” It's the story of the lawyers who fought for your privacy, the government that lied about spying on you, and the whistleblower who blew it all wide open. The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so pick up your copy today! Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast. Jarrod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it. Corinne Ruff is our story editor. We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman. The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.

item.title: ‘Strict liability’: The legal standard that could help rein in AI
item.description:
AI companies could be held liable for harm if courts treat the technology as abnormally dangerous, like explosives. Robert Nickelsberg via Getty ImagesSome people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting. In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued OpenAI, charging that it’s ChatGPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide. The state of Kentucky later filed suit, claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation. Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused. Regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms, too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda. I am a former litigator and a professor of business law, and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm. But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability. Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants. Abnormally dangerous software Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store. Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent or had no intent of creating trouble. A 2026 lawsuit claims ChatGPT encouraged a young woman to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity, such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it. AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “the utmost care to prevent the harm.” An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox – a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network – but loses control of it. The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose. One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage. Lawyers could make a strong case against so-called rogue AI that runs wild and isn’t available to most people. Applying the danger standard could still fail to rein in AI companies or reward victims appropriately. In 1929, aviation was seen as abnormally dangerous. But damages were capped at US$8,300, which was not a large deterrent. Attitudes changed in 1999, when the Montreal Convention standardized strict liability rules for international flights worldwide. It raised statutory damages and eliminated caps for negligence claims. Perhaps the most powerful tool in aviation liability today is for an authority to ground a company’s aircraft, which happened to Boeing after two fatal crashes with its 737 MAX planes. Guilty products Strict product liability is the other strategy for holding AI companies responsible for harm. In years past, courts tended to not see software as a product because it is intangible. But that view is shifting. In recent lawsuits alleging that social media hurt people, courts did see social media as a product and concluded that strict liability was applicable. Cases against Facebook have fallen into this category. Character.AI’s recent bankruptcy filing came in part because of a lawsuit in which the court treated the software as a product. “Design defects” is the part of the doctrine gaining traction. To use this, a plaintiff shows that the product posed a foreseeable risk to someone using it. So far, the doctrine has worked when applied to the lack of guardrails in chatbots. Pursuing strict liability could still run into snags. A court might order that AI software be turned off, or “grounded,” until it is improved. But as AI software creeps closer to being an operating system and is evermore embedded in everyone’s daily activities, it becomes difficult to suspend its use. Moving target AI software by its nature is constantly “learning” and therefore changing. It is impossible for a company to promise that AI software will absolutely behave a certain way. In many cases, AI software is inherently incapable of supporting a guarantee about design safety. Still, strict liability is a way to hold the maker responsible, “even when those products evolve in ways not specifically desired or foreseeable by their manufacturers,” according to a Brookings Institution report. I believe that if people are going to accept AI software as a boon to society, tough rules and sharp deterrents are needed. A strict liability system would shift risk from society to the companies seeking vast revenues. The next steps will be sorting out whether to treat all or some AI software as a product, and whether the technology is ultrahazardous. If it is treated as that dangerous, AI can develop with incentives to reduce harms and ensure that people injured are compensated. Deven Desai owns shares in Google, Inc. He received unrestricted research gifts from Google, Inc. and Facebook, Inc. a decade ago. He has not been employed by Google since 2010.

item.title: Pluralistic: Remembrance of proteins past (17 Nov 2026)
item.description: Today's links Remembrance of proteins past: People like what they like. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: BBC's bullshit DRM story; Radical hotel-room coffee independence; Foreclosure map predicts Trump vote; Pinkest pink v Anish Kapoor; Bruce Sterling on the Trump election; Keep the hope machine running; "Messy"; Jam To-Day; Billy Bragg x file-sharing; Second Life v copying; Best Buy claims copyright over prices; All cab conversations in Oxford must be recorded; The end of "software objectivity"; "Pirate Utopia"; Mamdani's photocopier-kicker; Biden does(n't) like SOPA; "The Freedom Maze"; Obama's weapons in Trump's hands; Gilmore/Barlow audio; MPAA v video iPods; RIP SF's neon Yahoo sign; NYC deputy mayor says no filming cops; Bannon wants to deport Indian CEOs; Academic economists charge $1k/h to defend giga-mergers; Iphones secretly spy on your calls; Office Depot fakes malware infections; Live Nation murdered at Astroworld; Games industry's self-induced brain injury. Upcoming appearances: Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Remembrance of proteins past (permalink) Without a doubt, the best piece of media from the 2026 midterms was Scott Colom's "Pick another senator instead" ad from his triumphant Mississippi senate campaign against GOP incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith: https://youtu.be/zpUnm09lTUk?si=3ApbHida5_VpQCLB&#038;t=2219 Some background: Colom is the first Black Mississippi senator elected since Reconstruction gave way to Jim Crow. He's also the first Democratic Mississippi senator since 1982. Colom's campaign shifted the statewide vote leftward by 19 points, and he won a quarter of the state's white votes. Colom ran a great campaign and promoted great policies, but also: he ran one of the great political ads of all time. That ad skewered Hyde-Smith's "let them eat whey powder" remark to WLOX Biloxi host Hugh Keeton, who asked her about the cost of living crisis and the high price of beef, to which she replied that people "have so many proteins to choose from": https://www.mississippifreepress.org/americans-who-cant-afford-beef-have-so-many-proteins-to-choose-from-says-us-sen-cindy-hyde-smith/ Colom's ad plays a montage of Mississippians expressing disgust with Hyde-Smith's response, saying "I'd rather choose another senator instead." Colom was quick to credit content creator Ryan Sayles, who joined the campaign after doing some freelance work for them, as the ad's mastermind: https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/12/ryan-sayles-scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-01163508 Much has been said about the ad's style, especially the viral "s-h-e-e-e-i-t" voiced by US Army vet Russ Hudson, who stepped in to do the ad when his father declined to curse on camera: https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-mississippi-senate But the most important analysis on the ad is of its substance, specifically how it repudiates one of the key doctrines of neoliberal, austerity economics, as David Dayen writes for The American Prospect: https://prospect.org/2026/11/16/how-the-mississippi-senate-win-exposed-austerity-logic/ Neoliberalism is the signature achievement of the "law and economics" movement that came out of the University of Chicago. The central conceit of law and econ is that economics is a "hard science" (not a social science) and that its domain is a deterministic, quantifiable physics of human behavior. Economists went so far as to create a fake "Nobel Prize" in economics in a bid to elevate their work out of the social sciences: https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics This "science" claims it can replace squishy, qualitative questions with mathematical models that can output the objectively correct answer to every thorny political question, thereby substituting an obscure form of mathematics for political deliberation: https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/03/all-models-are-wrong/#some-are-useful This is a remarkably cheap and transparent stunt. To produce this "mathematics of human behavior," you must first quantize all the qualitative questions so that they can be plugged into variables in econ equations. But here's the problem: assigning a numeric value to a qualitative factor is a qualitative exercise! When an economist decides that the pain you'll experience as a result of their policy prescriptions is worth "7" while the benefit is worth "8," they are not doing objective work, they're just declaring their own judgments (and biases) to be empirical observations, while demoting your judgments to mere "feelings" (and biases): https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics Economism doesn't just eliminate qualitative questions from policymaking: it incinerates all of those qualitative factors so that economists can perform mathematics on whatever dubious quantitative residue remains in the crucible: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-qualia/ This is where Scott Colom's brilliant campaign ad comes in. As Dayen points out, when Hyde-Smith made her "many other proteins to choose from," gaffe, she was referencing a key piece of economic theory that has been thoroughly weaponized by the neoliberals: "substitution." On its face, substitution is just the commonsense proposition that when prices for one good or service go up, some consumers will substitute another. When gas prices go up, more people ride the bus. When Instagram increases its ad-load, more people switch to Mastodon or Bluesky. When your ISP jacks up your price, you might switch to another carrier. So far, so good. Indeed, one of the best things about digital products and services is how low digital "switching costs" (the cost you bear when switching from one service to another) can be. The lower the switching costs are, the easier it is to substitute one thing for another. This means that, in a state of nature, tech bosses have to be careful about enshittifying their products, lest their users defect to a rival. This is why tech bosses have spent decades doing everything they can to jack up those "switching costs." They want to convert all their users into hostages: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/08/facebooks-secret-war-switching-costs Substitution is real and it makes sense. The problem comes when neoliberal economists use this idea in policy. In the early 2010s, Barack Obama proposed applying substitution to the American welfare system through something called "Chained CPI." "CPI" stands for the "Consumer Price Index": this is a measurement of the cost of a "basket of goods" (a bunch of supposedly representative household items) that is used to make inflationary adjustments to a variety of payments. When the CPI goes up, so do social security, welfare and disability payments. Otherwise, inflation would continually reduce the living standards of everyone who receives these entitlements. "Chained CPI" takes the CPI and applies substitution to it. Rather than asking whether hamburger just got more expensive, the economists who calculate CPI ask whether the cheapest protein at the grocery store got more expensive (because hamburger can be swapped out for another protein). Chained CPI's intent and effect is to reduce payments to retirees, disabled people, and poor people. Chained CPI is always going to be lower than CPI, because chained CPI only rises when the cheapest "substitute" for one of the items in CPI's "basket of goods" gets more expensive. In effect, the "basket of goods" becomes a transdimensional basket, one that contains every substitute good that might have gone into the basket in all possible parallel universes. Economists get to universe-shop for the dimension where that basket has the lowest cost, and then we all have to live in their chosen universe. Obama tried to adopt it 2013 as part of a "grand bargain" to reduce the deficit, but was thwarted by the Tea Party Caucus, who refused the grand bargain on the grounds that it contained an infinitesimal tax rise for the richest Americans: https://abcnews.com/blogs/politics/2013/04/obamas-chained-cpi-throws-off-pols-and-heres-how-it-works/ But chained CPI is one of the most cherished ideas of neoliberal thinktanks, so it came back in 2017 for Trump's tax giveaway to the super-rich, whose costs were partially offset by using chained CPI to calculate tax brackets, the standard deduction, and the Earned Income Tax Credit: https://newrepublic.com/article/145688/biggest-trojan-horse-republican-tax-plan As Dayen writes, "[This created] a regressive tax increase by eroding deductions and credits and pushing people into higher tax brackets. The wealthy were unaffected by this since they were already in the highest tax bracket and itemized rather than using the standard deduction." Which brings me back to Cindy Hyde-Smith's foot-in-mouth remarks about "so many proteins." Whether or not Hyde-Smith knew it, she was referencing this substitution/chained CPI doctrine when she told people that beef inflation didn't matter because other proteins were available. In doing so, she was performing economism's cheapest trick: pretending that her opinions are objective facts, while other people's opinions are just feelings. As Dayen writes, "[W]ho decides whether the cheaper product they switch to is 'similar' to the one that’s become so expensive that the consumer must give it up?&#8230;The logic is, approximately: You're not doing as badly as you think, so pick another protein and quit your whining." People do substitute one thing for another as a matter of economic necessity. But the idea that a "substitute" is an "equivalent" can only be accepted if you first buy into the economist's conceit that all qualitative matters can be safely incinerated, leaving the expert to do math on the quantitative ash. In this conceit, if you can't afford hamburgers and end up substituting chicken or fish, then you've found a new protein and have lost no "welfare." If you think otherwise, then you are expressing an irrational preference (unlike economists, whose preference for having a Nobel prize of their own is so empirically correct that it could be detected by a Martian peering at Earth through a telescope). It's not only Cindy Hyde-Smith who unconsciously metabolized the idea of substitution as "rationality"; it's the voters, too, who recognized in Hyde-Smith's remarks the arrogance of policy elites who've spent decades discounting their views as "feelings" while declaring their own views to be experimental validated facts. Not only do voters recognize this move: they hate it. They know that elites are perfectly capable of expressing strong views about qualitative matters and moving heaven and Earth to achieve a life that fits with their aesthetics. They know that the same Ivy League economists who dismiss their preferences as "irrational" will revel for 4,000 pages' worth of Marcel Proust expounding on the spiritual, intangible reasons for choosing his favorite baked goods. Economics is the study of why people do things, but somewhere along the way it became a club used to force people to do the things that powerful people prefer. The (alleged) "rationalism" of economism has worn out its welcome. You don't need an economics degree to understand why that "rationalism" is a cheap trick: after 50 years of neoliberalism, a Martian with a telescope could spot it. item.title: European Commission Plan to Give Frontex Trusted Flagger Status Is A Threat to Free Speech
item.description:
EFF and 27 other human rights organizations called on the European Commission today to retract a dangerous proposal granting its border agency Frontex to request that national authorities issue takedown orders for social media content and giving it “trusted flagger” status under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU regulation governing online platforms and content moderation in the region.The extraordinarily improper proposal not only disregards the provisions of the DSA but also places a mechanism of enforcement overreach in the hands of a law enforcement agency that has failed to safeguard people against serious human rights violations at EU borders.Under the proposal, Frontex has the power to “monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant to external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.” Granting Frontex trusted flagger privileges on top of its existing mandate risks creating a powerful mechanism for over-enforcement, stifling the free expression of migrants, asylum seekers, and other marginalized groups. We warned the Commission of these risks in a letter.The DSA is supposed to make online platforms more accountable and protect users’ fundamental rights, not give the EU power to sic its border police on people for exercising their right to free expression.EFF and other rights organizations have for years sounded alarms about potential abuse under the DSA’s trusted flagger provision, which gives “Digital Services Coordinators” the ability to award entities—including law enforcement agencies—a privileged channel to alert online platforms about illegal content. We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content. In July, we told the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers. The EU proposal gives Frontex decision-making power over free expression that is not envisaged under the DSA. First, content removal orders can only be issued by relevant national authorities. The DSA does not foresee a role for entities like Frontex to request such orders. Second, trusted flaggers notify platforms of suspected illegal content—platforms must prioritize these notices and they have sole responsibility to decide to remove content. It’s not flaggers’ role to request removal orders from national authorities. Combining these powers blur enforcement and flagging functions, which the Commission’s own draft guidelines on trusted flaggers explicitly caution against. “The risk of Frontex utilizing its power as both a Trusted Flagger and authority that can demand removal orders, to surveil user-generated speech, and over-flag content under the guise of ‘border security risk’ is clear. This will likely result in platforms over-censoring content and chilling the speech of already marginalized groups, particularly those from migrant and asylum-seeking communities,” the letter says. We urge the Commission to rescind the proposal. It undermines the DSA, threatens fundamental rights of citizens and non-citizens, and is enforcement overreach that does not align with international human rights standards.

Source feed: https://www.eff.org/rss/updates.xml

item.title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
item.description:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches. Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred. While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems. Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code. Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework: STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)1, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors. LIABILITY: The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system ENFORCEMENT: Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action. The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools. 1NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of voluntary practices for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

item.title: Donate Equity to Support Digital Rights: Stocks, DAFs, and Giving
item.description:
Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit? For 35 years, the Electronic Frontier Foundation has been advancing our digital rights, including defending security researchers, encrypting the web, and fighting illegal surveillance. Donating equity to EFF can help support this important work. Perhaps your family has taken advantage of the new tax law around giving by creating a Donor-Advised Fund. Perhaps your employer has gone public and you now own stock. Perhaps you’ve seen some of EFF’s recent successes and thought, Man, imagine what they could do with more. Stocks A gift of equity can help your contribution go farther and offer tax savings. When you donate appreciated stock, you avoid paying capital gains tax on any increase in its value. You also receive a charitable income tax deduction for the fair market value of appreciated stock on the date it is transferred. Also, more and more companies are offering gift-matching programs that can double your impact at no additional cost. If you have owned the stock for less than a year, your gift will not qualify for all of these potential tax advantages. And gifts of appreciated stock are fully deductible—up to a maximum of 30% of your adjusted gross income. Please check with your accountant or tax advisor regarding your particular tax status. We have helpful information here to facilitate the transfer of securities. Please email us if you have any questions. And let us know in advance if you are transferring securities. We’ll need to know the amount and type of shares that you will be donating in order to provide a tax receipt. Donor-Advised Funds As a 501(c)(3) organization, EFF can also receive distributions through your Donor-Advised Fund (DAF), including one-time gifts or recurring donations. Simply inform your DAF provider you would like to make a gift to: Electronic Frontier Foundation (EIN 04-3091431) 815 Eddy Street San Francisco, CA 94109 Please note that many DAF providers do not provide the donor’s name to the recipient organization. If you would like to be recognized for your gift, let us know the amount of the gift and the fund name. And due to IRS regulations, we may not be able to provide a thank you gift in line with your giving level. The DAF provider is responsible for your tax receipt. JOIN EFF The rules that govern technology shape our freedom. Help us write those rules today!

item.title: Amazon Ring’s New Indoor Surveillance Drone Is Not Compatible with Privacy
item.description:
Amazon Ring has finally announced their long-dreaded indoor drone, a small flying surveillance device connected to their security suite of products that can fly around your house filming and recording things. The device is supposedly designed to fly preset paths across your home and will also activate if a sensor or alarm has been triggered. Customers should think twice about purchasing these devices for a number of reasons. These devices are problematic in many of the ways we’ve said Ring’s stationary home surveillance products are a problem, plus some new ways. At a very basic level, they are essentially a window into your house that can be accessed by anyone with access to your account—which has historically included bad actors looking to embarrass or harass Ring users and employees of the company. What’s worse, Ring has supercharged the units with its ‘AI Pilot’ to map routes, model the interior of the home, and control movement. This means not only is the footage being sent to corporate servers, but the company is also making inferences about your home to carry out tasks. How much home usage data this is based on, and if it can be used to infer when certain household activities are happening, are both open questions. And presumably, to maintain the preset routes, inferred data about your home will still be held by Ring even after any stored video footage is deleted. The risk to your privacy is only compounded once you consider Ring’s renewed partnership with police through the massive surveillance and taser vendor, Axon. Through this partnership, police have the ability to request camera footage from Ring users with just a few clicks on Axon’s platforms. This includes its Fusus platform, an interactive surveillance feed and map police use to manage all the surveillance devices they have access to, like automated license plate readers. It’s unclear exactly what devices police can request footage from, but if this request feature is extended to Ring’s drones, police could easily send requests for footage from inside your house. Sharing is voluntary, but once footage is submitted, it cannot be retracted. Worse still, if your footage is not sitting on Amazon’s servers fully encrypted—and there’s reason to believe their privacy options are not the strongest—police could serve a warrant straight to the company, instead of to you, to get footage from your devices. New problems and questions arise because the camera can fly. For instance: if police serve a warrant on Amazon, can they only get the footage from the camera, or could they also get access to control the drone? If the latter, we could be looking at the first full home search in history where police serve a warrant on a third-party tech company and not the resident. The CEO of Ring has pitched this product’s safety benefits in several ways, including by saying: “If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window...You’re probably not going to go into that house.” But partially justifying a $250 piece of technology that invades your privacy on what an imagined burglar might do doesn’t sound like a foundation for safety—it sounds like security theater and marketing. It isn’t new for Ring to prey on the fears and paranoia of people and their properties. This is the latest iteration of that: a patrolling drone or rover wouldn't have been possible even in the world's top museums and art galleries a generation ago. Moving this technology into the household as a common consumer product is another example of companies attempting to lower the bar on surveillance being normalized. With previous Ring products, consumers have had to consider what cameras and high-powered microphones can learn about their home usage from the front door. Autonomous flying drones and rovers inside the home add a whole new layer. What can these devices learn about you and your family? And do you really trust that data sitting on a server somewhere? Consumers should consider these risks before subjecting their guests and households to the latest creepy surveillance tool.

Source feed: https://www.eff.org/rss/updates.xml

item.title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)
item.description:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long. Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game. Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense. Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too. Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control, and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products. Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them. Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon. There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right? With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google's blog post notes that it has whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places. But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today. No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers. The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use. Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy. Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby: “And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.” What We Can Do About It It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel. Of course, that doesn’t mean we all just have to sit around and hope that’s what happens. For its part, Apple launched its Audio Intelligence features in beta specifically to get feedback, and we think it’s worth taking the time to fill out their feedback forms (or in the Feedback Assistant app if you’re in the beta) and let them know what you think. Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

item.title: Pluralistic: I told you so (13 Nov 2026)
item.description: Today's links I told you so: Microsoft is too big to live. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Canada's corrupt copyright czar; Universal Music CEO v iPod owners; Berlusconi x neo-fascists; Balancing 3,118 coins on a dime; All for-profit healthcare is a problem. Upcoming appearances: Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. I told you so (permalink) Here's the one weird trick that made it possible for monopolies to conquer the world: the antitrust bar changed the rules so that it was impossible to prove whether a company had formed an illegal monopoly, and then these rules meant that monopolies were almost never challenged, and what challenges did arise were usually unsuccessful, and even the successful challenges resulted in meaningless "penalties" that left monopolists unscathed. Every policy has three important dimensions: substance, scope and administrability: "Substance" is what the policy actually says. For example, the basic substance of copyright law is, "You can't display, transmit or reproduce a copyrighted work without permission." "Scope" is when the policy gets applied. When copyright law was formulated, the key activities it regulated all required a bunch of expensive industrial equipment. Every book implied a printing press, every record implied a record-pressing plant, every film implied a film duplication lab. That meant that, by default, pretty much the only people who had to care about what copyright law said were industrial actors &#8211; firms who might reasonably be expected to also have access to a lawyer. That matters a lot to administrability. "Administrability" is what it takes to actually administer the policy. Can you detect potential violations, and when you do, how hard is it to figure out whether the rule was actually broken? Again, in the pre-digital era, it was pretty easy to spot copyright violations: pirate books, records and movies are tangible, physical objects, and distributing them requires advertisement, delivery and payment. After detecting an infringement, copyright enforcers must resolve a further question: whether a display, transmission or copy fall under "fair use." Fair use is a "fact intensive" rule, one that requires a lot of evidence and argument to adjudicate. It's almost impossible to categorically rule in or rule out a specific use as "fair": https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/27/nuke-first/#ask-questions-never Despite the complexity and expense of determining fair use, pre-digital copyright was still relatively administrable, because fair use questions themselves were relatively rare. Most fair uses (for example, photocopying part of a book for classroom use) were below the threshold for detection by rightsholders, so these questions almost never found their way into court. The fair use questions that did get to court were big, splashy affairs, like whether it's okay to rewrite a famous pro-slavery novel from the enslaved characters' perspective (it is!): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Done_Gone There are a lot of legal questions that require nuance, fact-finding and argumentation to resolve, and that's not necessarily a problem. It's fine to apply these complicated, lengthy processes to things that only happen every once in a while. Take probate: most of us will die one or fewer times, so it's not the worst thing in the world that figuring out what happens to our stuff when that happens can involve some legal complexity. But as media went digital, copyright's scope expanded dramatically. "Making or handling copies of copyrighted work" stopped being an industrial activity that implied a complex business and access to legal expertise. The only thing a digital computer does is make and handle copies, so every time any ordinary person clicks their mouse, dozens of potentially thorny copyright questions arise. What's more, those questions involve the public internet, which raises the number of potential infringements that a rightsholder can detect (and potentially seek legal redress for) from dozens to millions. Nearly all of these potential infringements fall under fair use, but fair use is a fact-intensive doctrine suited to resolving occasional disputes between large firms. Fair use is monumentally unsuited to resolving questions that arise hundreds of times every day for nearly every person alive, including small children and other people who almost certainly can't get legal advice: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-a-new-deal-for-copyright/ This is how copyright broke: new technology (digital computers) radically expanded its scope, conscripting everyone into using copyright's framework for everyday activities that had nothing to do with the media industry's supply-chain. That framework was developed for industrial actors with access to lawyers, and its most important aspect (fair use) is a fact-intensive doctrine that takes serious work to resolve, but now had to be navigated many times every day by every person. So copyright became unadministrable: you can't apply a fact-intensive doctrine to everyday activities undertaken by everyday people. If you try, you will make criminals of everyone. It would be literally impossible to train enough copyright lawyers to advise every person every time they use a computer to do something that might violate copyright law. Back to antitrust: when the pro-monopoly partisans of the "law and economy" movement set out to neuter antitrust, they deliberately introduced a set of hurdles that were designed to make it impossible to administer competition law. First, they introduced an "intent" standard: it was no longer enough for a company to have a monopoly, the company must have intended to secure and maintain that monopoly. If you want to be sure a law doesn't get enforced, this is a fantastic standard to apply. After all, how can anyone know what anyone else intended? Ask any anthropologist and they'll tell you: the only way to find out what someone intends by their actions is to ask them, and even that only works if you can trust them to answer honestly: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thick_description#Clifford_Geertz If antitrust law can only be enforced by mind-readers and advanced philosophers who have solved the intersubjectivity problem, then antitrust law can't be enforced at all: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersubjective_verifiability But that wasn't all! Antitrust's enemies insisted on another fact-intensive question: "market definition." They made the (seemingly commonsense) point that if a company is said to have a monopoly, we must first determine which thing the company has monopolized. This sounds like a no-brainer, but it's actually a way to introduce unresolvable, show-stopper arguments into any antitrust enforcement action. Take Amazon: the company's ecommerce monopoly is obvious to anyone who hasn't been in a coma for the past 15 years. But when Amazon gets investigated for this monopoly, they will insist that they don't participate in the "ecommerce" economy, but rather in "the buying and selling of things in general." Then they point out that people still go to the corner store for a pint of milk, still buy a pack of gum from the kiosk at the train-station, and still buy some hair-gel from the barber after a trim, and therefore Amazon can't possibly have a monopoly. "Market definition" is a playground for bad-faith semanticians. Luckily for the world's monopolists, the very existence of this legal doctrine has conjured up an army of bad-faith semanticians, most of them with expensive Ivy League economics degrees, who make millions coming up with bizarre market definition arguments that can draw out any legal proceeding for years, often to the point where there is a change in government and the federal prosecutors just walk away from the case. Taken together, these impossible fact-intensive questions would be enough to bury antitrust, but then came the final blow: frequency. Once capital had won the battle to mire antitrust cases in questions that take years and millions to resolve, they embarked on a frenzy of monopolistic mergers. This meant that the kind of antitrust questions that originally arose every few years were suddenly coming up several times per month. This was the killer combo: making antitrust a plodding ball-ache of thorny philosophical and technical questions, and then rigging the system so that these questions arise in a nonstop flurry guaranteed that antitrust would fail. That's what happened with Microsoft. The company had a 95% desktop OS market-share when Clinton's trustbusters dragged them into court. Nevertheless, the company played all kinds of "market definition" games that dragged the case out for years. They also insisted that they never intended to form a monopoly, despite smoking-gun memos about "sucking up all the market oxygen": https://web.archive.org/web/20190717023522/https://www.justice.gov/atr/department-justice-7 This dragged on so long that even after Microsoft lost its case, the appeal carried on until after GW Bush stole the presidency, and then his DoJ walked away from the case, letting Microsoft continue to enjoy (and increase) its monopoly: https://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/07/business/us-vs-microsoft-overview-us-abandoning-its-effort-break-apart-microsoft-saying.html What happened next should not come as a surprise to anyone. Microsoft got convicted of deliberately setting out to create a monopoly, and then paid no penalty. After an all-too-brief period of post-traumatic good behavior, Microsoft returned to its monopolistic ways. Along the way, Microsoft sucked up to a succession of presidential administrations, culminating in the company's emergence as a de facto wing of the Trump regime. Microsoft's CEO paid $1m to sit on the inaugural dais, and then directed the company to donate millions to the Epstein Ballroom, and then provided the IT services for ICE's ethnic cleansing pogroms: https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/us-ice-triples-use-of-microsoft-cloud-in-six-months/#:~:text=ICE%20has%20been,first%20presidential%20term. Microsoft isn't merely the in-house IT shop for Trump's domestic agenda: they've also weaponized foreign reliance on Microsoft's cloud apps and they punish foreign officials who thwart Trump abroad: https://www.theregister.com/off-prem/2026/02/18/microsoft-throws-spox-under-the-bus-in-icc-email-flap/ When forced, Microsoft candidly admits that no matter where in the world your Microsoft data is stored, when it comes to foreign firms and governments, the company will give warrantless, secret access to their data to Trump's cronies: https://www.theregister.com/off-prem/2025/07/25/microsoft-exec-admits-it-cannot-guarantee-data-sovereignty/458553 All of this raises an urgent digital sovereignty question: what if Microsoft (a monopolist that is entirely dependent on Trump's favor to keep it free of existential legal problems) cuts off your country's Office 365 access? This is the question I raised late last year in my CCC talk about the "Post-American Internet": https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition (Coming soon in expanded form to a bookstore near you:) https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374623845/thepostamericaninternet/ And now, Microsoft has given the whole world a preview of how this might play out, because their servers have collapsed, shutting the world off from Outlook email, Azure cloud, Copilot, Teams, and other key offerings: https://www.bbc.com/news/live/cq5y10ge3dp3t The outage lasted for about two days, and around the world, government agencies and businesses large and small ground to a halt. Without Office 365, Outlook and Teams, many organizations could not even convene a meeting or formulate a plan to deal with the outage. All of this raises an important question: is Microsoft guilty of negligence, and, if so, what should be done about this? Here's my answer: yes, Microsoft is presumptively guilty of negligence, and any response to this must include antitrust breakups of the company. Here's why I think that. Microsoft has demonstrably underinvested in its IT stability. Any IT plan that results in a global, multi-day outage is, by definition, inadequate. Whether the problem could have been solved by buying more servers, or hiring more people, or changing the management of key divisions is immaterial. Every one of these measures &#8211; every single measure that could have prevented this &#8211; costs money. By not spending that money, Microsoft definitively underinvested in its products. But Microsoft doesn't lack for funds! Microsoft is a convicted monopolist, and it has the margins to prove it. In 2025-2026, the company pissed away more than $30b in stock buybacks, a once-illegal (and still sleazy) form of stock manipulation. Over that same period, Microsoft lost nearly $200b on AI ventures that it now admits will not pay off: https://www.cnbc.com/2025/02/24/microsoft-reiterates-plan-to-invest-80-billion-in-ai-.html Then there's the layoffs. 2026 saw Microsoft's first-ever voluntary retirement buyout, which served as the overture to a year that saw a 25% headcount cut &#8211; 60,000 employees slated for destruction: https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/microsoft-buyout-offers-ai-cuts Ever had a boss who caught you catching your breath and shoved a broom in your hand, barking, "If you have time to lean, you have time to clean?" That goes quintuple for convicted monopolists who bring the global economy to a halt due to a multi-day outage. If you can't manage to keep your servers online, you have no business incinerating tens of billions on stock buybacks, much less hundreds of billions to feed the AI money-furnace. Did Microsoft need the tens of thousands of workers it threw away? Demonstrably so: when they were on the payroll, Microsoft's servers were up. Now they're gone, and so are the servers. It doesn't matter how those workers related to this specific outage: if you can't keep your servers online, you either don't have enough site reliability engineers, or you don't have enough managers to deploy them effectively, or you don't have enough managers to hire the managers and SREs you need. Q.E.D. This is all characteristic of the monopolist's pathology. The problem with monopolists is that they have pricing power and market power: the power to foist inferior products on their customers and degraded working conditions on their employees and unfair terms on their suppliers. Microsoft's hundreds of billions in wastage and tens of thousands of layoffs are a massive transfer of value from customers, workers and suppliers to investors. The fact that the company judged (correctly, it seems) that they could make us all eat shit and we'd ask for second helpings is a nice, clean proof of monopoly power. Here, I think, is a nice, bright-line, administrable test for monopoly power. If your company has a dominant position and if it allocates its surplus capital to its investors and if that precedes a significant degradation of your products, then you have an illegal monopoly and you should be broken up. We don't need to inquire as to whether you have a wicked heart that intentionally set about to create a monopoly, nor do we have to argue endlessly about how many angels can dance on the head of your market definition. If you think you are so powerful that you can fuck up your products and not suffer as a result then you are too big to care, and that is simply too big. This isn't the only fix we need to antitrust law, but it is a fix that would specifically let us target Big Tech. Microsoft is a living, breathing (limping, gasping) repudiation of the thesis that monopolies are efficient and if we only let them amass endless market share and profits, they will use their "economies of scale" to deliver superior products. It's not that economies of scale don't exist, but for companies to take advantage of these economies of scale, they have to be motivated to expend their capital to do so. The more powerful a company is, the less inclined it will be to apportion capital to workers, suppliers and consumers, and the more it will cheat us all to enrich its shareholders. We can't afford to let this crisis go to waste. Google was convicted of creating and maintaining a monopoly three times over the past couple years and every single time the judge decided the company should not face any real punishment for that monopoly, on the basis that the monopoly is what lets Google deliver such excellence for us. Does anyone still think Google is excellent? How about Apple? Google pays Apple an annual bribe of more than $20b to stay out of the search market. Judge Amit Mehta decided to let Google continue paying this bribe to Apple so that Apple would have the capital it needed to deliver excellent products. Apple promptly went on to have a string of catastrophically bad product launches &#8211; while throwing away $170b manipulating its share-price with stock buybacks: https://finance.yahoo.com/news/apple-dodged-a-20-billion-hit-thanks-to-google-antitrust-ruling-163056806.html Both companies are demonstrably underinvesting in quality in order to divert R&#38;D and product maintenance capital to their shareholders. They are too big to care. In this age of nonstop mergers and acquisitions, we can't afford to make merger approval turn on fact-intensive questions, but we can sure as hell create this administrable, bright-line test for whether a merger should be unwound after the fact. Did your company buy another company and then enshittify both products? Great, now we're breaking you up, and your investors are getting fucked. Maybe next time they'll fire the board when they announce another stupid, anti-competitive merger. Microsoft is too big in every way. Too big to fail, too big to jail and too big to care. Too big to trust. Too big to rely upon. Too big to foster a corporate culture that cares about reliability, a decent workplace, or product quality. There's a straight line from GW Bush's decision to let Microsoft skate in 2001 and the situation a quarter century later, where Microsoft is a load-bearing piece of the world's most important firms and government agencies, and where this means that Microsoft knows that it can throw away tens of thousands of workers and hundreds of billions of dollars, crash the planet, and wake up tomorrow unscathed, ready to do it all over again. item.title: So Long, Jensen
item.description:
AI The parents of a girl is suing Google over its Gemini AI platform, saying that the chatbot helped the girl plan her own suicide and funeral (the plans were found before the girl went through with them) and gave her advice on how to keep her plans secret from her family [NY Times ($) | Reuters] Three men have been indicted in federal court for impersonating CEOS at various companies via AI deepfakes of images and voices to steal millions of dollars [The Guardian ($) | NY Times | DOJ press release | Indictment]A federal judge in Kentucky has found that qualified immunity does not
